analysis.one_liner: Caps interest and fees on consumer credit at 36% a year, ending triple-digit payday and overdraft rates.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set a national ceiling of 36% a year on the combined interest and fees lenders charge consumers, counting late fees, overdraft fees, credit insurance, and add-on products toward the total. It covered payday loans, car-title loans, bank overdraft lines, and credit cards, closed loopholes lenders use to export high rates across state lines, and backed the cap with criminal penalties and enforcement by state attorneys general. Today millions of borrowers pay roughly 400% annual interest on payday loans and up to 3,500% on overdraft, and the bill was written to end that.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who use high-cost credit: payday borrowers paying about 400% annual interest, car-title borrowers paying about 300%, and bank customers hit with overdraft fees that can run to 3,500% annualized. The bill would have voided illegal loan agreements and forced creditors to return principal, interest, and fees on violating transactions, and let state attorneys general sue violators.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the all-in cost of consumer credit — interest plus every fee charged as a condition of the loan — at 36% a year, with no exceptions and no agency authority to waive it.
Counts late fees, overdraft fees, cash-advance fees, credit insurance premiums, and ancillary add-on products toward the cap, so lenders cannot dodge the limit by relabeling interest as fees.

Makes any loan made in violation of the cap void and unenforceable, requires the creditor to return all principal, interest, and fees collected, and imposes up to a year in prison and a fine of the greater of $50,000 or three times the accrued debt per violation.

Lets state attorneys general sue to enforce the cap and leaves stronger state rate caps in place, and replaces the APR disclosure on billing statements with a single 'FAIR' rate showing the full cost.

The bill's findings cite the 2006 federal 36% cap for servicemembers, which curbed payday, car-title, and tax-refund lending around military bases, as proof the approach works, and estimate consumers pay about $17 billion a year in high-cost overdraft charges and up to $7 billion for storefront and online payday loans.

analysis.who_pays: High-cost lenders and the banks that collect overdraft and cash-advance fee revenue would lose the income: payday and car-title lenders whose business model is triple-digit rates, and banks collecting billions in overdraft and cash-advance fees. Credit card issuers whose combined interest, annual, late, and over-limit fees would exceed 36% would also be constrained. Some borrowers who currently rely on high-cost loans, even at painful rates, could lose access to that credit if lenders exit rather than lend at the cap.

drawbacks.text: A hard 36% all-in cap could cut off small-dollar credit for some borrowers with poor credit histories: if lenders will not lend at the capped rate, those borrowers are left with no loan at all rather than a cheaper one, which is why the bill itself calls for encouraging alternatives like no-fee small-dollar installment loans.

The penalties are unusually severe for consumer-credit law — up to one year in prison and a fine of the greater of $50,000 or three times the accrued debt for each violation — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge as a heavy-handed enforcement tool.

Banks and card issuers argued-style objection: capping combined interest and fees below 36% for some cardholders and overdraft users would force those customers onto less convenient credit or eliminate overdraft lines they use, while the fee revenue banks currently book from these products — roughly $17 billion a year in overdraft charges by the bill's own estimate — would disappear rather than be returned to customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the borrowers the bill targets, the arithmetic is stark: rates of 300% to 3,500% versus 36%. The genuine tradeoff is at the margin — a strict cap may leave some subprime borrowers without a lender willing to serve them, and the criminal penalties are blunt. But the bill kept stronger state caps intact, offered a defensible benchmark already proven on military families since 2006, and directed regulators to police circumvention. The main reason it failed was not a flaw in the design; it never received any committee action at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on March 23, 2015 with five original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
That referral was the last action ever taken: the complete action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote for the remainder of the 114th Congress.
The bill attracted six cosponsors, all Democrats, and none of them sat in the majority controlling the Banking Committee's agenda.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-cost lenders and banks that collect overdraft and payday-style fee revenue are better off: they kept charging triple-digit rates, and the roughly $17 billion a year in overdraft charges and $7 billion in payday loan charges the bill's findings documented continued through the Congress and after.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its lead sponsor.

for.name: Sens. Barbara Boxer, Jeff Merkley, Richard Blumenthal, Sheldon Whitehouse

against.name: Sen. Richard Shelby
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Democrats, and the Republican-chaired Banking Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: Their business model is charging roughly 300% to 400% annual interest on small short-term loans; a hard 36% all-in cap with criminal penalties would end it. Borrowers who currently use these loans would benefit from the cap but could face reduced access if lenders exit.

The bill counts overdraft fees, cash-advance fees, and not-sufficient-funds fees toward the 36% cap, threatening an estimated $17 billion a year in overdraft charges; a bank charging up to 3,500% annualized on overdraft could not continue under this bill.

Issuers whose combined interest, annual, late, and over-limit fees exceed 36% of balances would have to reprice, cutting fee income; cardholders with good credit paying under the cap would be largely unaffected. The CRS summary describes the cap applying to open-end credit plans (credit cards).

industries.industry: Consumer Credit Protection Bureau and state attorneys general (enforcers)
industries.note: The bill would give the CFPB rulemaking authority over the cap's calculations and give state attorneys general a new three-year enforcement action with injunctive relief, expanding their toolkit against high-cost lending.
